--- title: "Leakage-Aware Modeling of NBA Game Outcomes Using Rolling Performance Metrics" subtitle: "Revised version" author: "Kaleb Coleman" date: last-modified date-format: "MMMM YYYY" setup: "" abstract: | I predict whether the home team wins an NBA regular-season game using only information available before tip-off: lagged rolling means of team box-score efficiency and pre-game Elo ratings. Models are trained on 2002--2025 and tested on the 2025--26 season, which no earlier version of this project used. A ridge logistic regression on rolling features plus Elo reaches 68.6% accuracy and an AUC of 0.738 on that season, against 55.4% for always picking the home team. A two-variable Elo model does almost as well (67.9%, AUC 0.731), and the 95% bootstrap interval for the AUC gain from adding rolling features includes zero. This revision also corrects three problems in the course version: cross-validation that mixed future and past seasons, a classification threshold tuned on the test season, and an incomplete data pull. format: html: toc: true number-sections: true other-links: - text: PDF version href: paper.pdf pdf: documentclass: article papersize: letter geometry: margin=1in fontsize: 11pt number-sections: true colorlinks: true cite-method: biblatex biblio-style: authoryear keep-tex: false fig-pos: "htbp" include-in-header: text: | \usepackage{booktabs} bibliography: references.bib execute: echo: false warning: false message: false --- ::: {.cell} ::: # Introduction Box-score statistics from a game describe that game. Using them to predict the same game's result is leakage: the model sees information that would not exist at prediction time, and its accuracy looks better than it is [@kaufman2012leakage]. The same problem appears in evaluation when a model is validated on games that happened before the games it was trained on. This project builds pre-game features from team box scores, checks in code that no feature uses the game it describes or any later game, and evaluates models in time order. It asks two questions: 1. How much better than "the home team wins" can pre-game rolling efficiency metrics predict single-game outcomes? 2. Do those metrics add anything beyond a simple Elo rating [@elo1978rating]? # Data Team box scores come from `hoopR::load_nba_team_box()` [@gilani2021hoopr], which serves ESPN box scores compiled by the SportsDataverse project. I keep regular-season games between the 30 current franchises for the 2001--02 through 2025--26 seasons (labeled 2002--2026 by season end year). The snapshot used here was pulled on October 28, 2026. ::: {.cell tbl-cap='Games per season in the modeling data. 2002--2004 had 29 teams (1,189 games); 2012 (lockout), 2020, and 2021 were shortened.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Season | Games|Season | Games| |:------|-----:|:------|-----:| |2002 | 1,189|2015 | 1,230| |2003 | 1,189|2016 | 1,230| |2004 | 1,189|2017 | 1,229| |2005 | 1,230|2018 | 1,229| |2006 | 1,230|2019 | 1,230| |2007 | 1,230|2020 | 1,059| |2008 | 1,230|2021 | 1,080| |2009 | 1,230|2022 | 1,230| |2010 | 1,230|2023 | 1,230| |2011 | 1,230|2024 | 1,231| |2012 | 990|2025 | 1,231| |2013 | 1,224|2026 | 1,231| |2014 | 1,229| | | ::: ::: After dropping each team's first game of every season (where no rolling history exists), 29,637 games remain. The home team won 58.5% of games from 2002 to 2025, but that share has fallen over time (@fig-home), which matters for any model trained on all past seasons. ![Share of regular-season games won by the home team.](../figures/home_advantage.png){#fig-home width=90%} # Features **Per-game efficiency.** For each team and game I compute possessions and the standard rate statistics [@oliver2004basketball; @kubatko2007starting]: effective field-goal percentage, true shooting percentage, free-throw rate, three-point attempt rate, offensive and defensive rating, net rating, offensive and defensive rebound percentage, and turnover percentage. **Lagged rolling means.** For a window of $w \in \{3, 5, 10\}$ games, the feature for a team's game $t$ is the mean of that statistic over the team's games $t-w$ to $t-1$ in the same season. The current game is never included, and windows reset at the start of each season, so the first game of a season has no value. **Matchup features.** Each game gets the home and away team's rolling values, plus home-minus-away differences and home/away ratios for rebounding and turnover rates. **Elo.** Ratings start at 1500, use $K = 20$ and a 100-point home advantage, and are updated after each game. The value attached to a game is the rating *before* that game. I keep two versions: one reset every season and one carried across seasons. **Checks.** The test suite (`tests/testthat/test-features.R`) confirms that each rolling value equals the mean of the previous $w$ games and that first games have no value. It also changes the result of one mid-season game and checks that no feature for that game, or any earlier game, changes, while later games do change. # Evaluation design All evaluation is in time order [@hyndman2021fpp3]. - **Validation (2015--2025).** For each season $s$, models are trained on all seasons before $s$ and predict $s$. This gives 11 out-of-sample seasons. - **Threshold.** The cutoff for calling a home win is chosen to maximize accuracy on the last validation season (2025), then applied unchanged to the holdout. - **Holdout (2026).** Models trained on 2002--2025 predict the 2025--26 season once (1,215 games). - **Penalty tuning.** For ridge and elastic net [@friedman2010glmnet], the penalty is chosen by cross-validation inside the training seasons, with folds made of whole seasons. - **Metrics.** Accuracy, AUC [@robin2011proc], Brier score [@brier1950verification], and log loss. Holdout intervals come from 2,000 bootstrap resamples of games [@efron1993bootstrap], including a paired interval for each model's AUC minus the Elo-only model's AUC. The models are: - **Majority:** always predict the training-set home-win rate. - **Logistic, Elo only:** season-reset and all-time Elo differences. - **Logistic, lean rolling:** five-game differences in net rating, offensive-minus-defensive rating, offensive rebound percentage, turnover percentage, and effective field-goal percentage. - **Ridge, rolling:** all rolling features (3, 5, and 10 games), no Elo. - **Ridge, rolling + Elo**, and **elastic net, rolling + Elo** ($\alpha \in \{0.25, 0.5, 0.75\}$). - **Gradient boosting** (xgboost; 400 trees of depth 3, learning rate 0.03) and a **neural net** (one hidden layer of 8 units, weight decay 0.1, inputs standardized), both on rolling features + Elo. Their settings are fixed defaults, not tuned, so they are a check on whether a nonlinear model finds structure the linear models miss rather than a tuned comparison. # Results ## Validation seasons ::: {.cell tbl-cap='Mean out-of-sample metrics over the 2015--2025 validation seasons (each season predicted by a model trained on all earlier seasons). Threshold 0.5.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Model | Accuracy| AUC| Brier| Log loss| |:--------------------------------|--------:|-----:|-----:|--------:| |Majority (home win rate) | 0.566| --| 0.246| 0.686| |Logistic: Elo only | 0.648| 0.697| 0.218| 0.625| |Logistic: lean rolling | 0.615| 0.645| 0.231| 0.654| |Ridge: rolling | 0.631| 0.670| 0.224| 0.640| |Ridge: rolling + Elo | 0.652| 0.699| 0.216| 0.621| |Elastic net: rolling + Elo | 0.651| 0.700| 0.216| 0.620| |Gradient boosting: rolling + Elo | 0.649| 0.698| 0.217| 0.623| |Neural net (MLP): rolling + Elo | 0.635| 0.669| 0.228| 0.647| ::: ::: Across the validation seasons, ridge with rolling features and Elo averaged an AUC of 0.699. The Elo-only logistic model averaged 0.697, and rolling features without Elo averaged 0.670. Season by season (@fig-validation), the full model had a higher AUC than Elo only in 8 of 11 seasons, and Elo only beat the rolling features without Elo in 11 of 11. ![Out-of-sample AUC by validation season. Each point is a season predicted by a model trained on all earlier seasons.](../figures/validation_auc_by_season.png){#fig-validation width=95%} ## Holdout season (2025--26) ::: {.cell tbl-cap='Holdout results for the 2025--26 season. Accuracy is shown at 0.5 and at the threshold chosen on the 2025 validation season. Intervals are 95% bootstrap percentile intervals.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Model | Acc. (0.5)| 95% CI| Acc. (val. thr.)| AUC| AUC 95% CI| Brier| |:--------------------------------|----------:|------------:|----------------:|-----:|------------:|-----:| |Majority (home win rate) | 0.554| 0.526--0.583| 0.554 (0.50)| --| --| 0.248| |Logistic: Elo only | 0.679| 0.651--0.706| 0.681 (0.56)| 0.731| 0.703--0.759| 0.208| |Logistic: lean rolling | 0.642| 0.615--0.670| 0.647 (0.57)| 0.683| 0.655--0.713| 0.223| |Ridge: rolling | 0.664| 0.638--0.691| 0.659 (0.55)| 0.712| 0.684--0.741| 0.214| |Ridge: rolling + Elo | 0.686| 0.662--0.712| 0.686 (0.55)| 0.738| 0.711--0.766| 0.205| |Elastic net: rolling + Elo | 0.686| 0.660--0.712| 0.690 (0.54)| 0.737| 0.709--0.765| 0.205| |Gradient boosting: rolling + Elo | 0.682| 0.656--0.709| 0.679 (0.55)| 0.733| 0.705--0.762| 0.207| |Neural net (MLP): rolling + Elo | 0.653| 0.627--0.679| 0.653 (0.53)| 0.709| 0.682--0.738| 0.222| ::: ::: ![Holdout AUC by model with 95% bootstrap intervals. The dashed line marks the Elo-only model.](../figures/model_comparison.png){#fig-models width=95%} On the holdout (@fig-models), ridge with rolling features and Elo predicted 68.6% of games correctly (AUC 0.738), compared with 55.4% for always picking the home team. The Elo-only model reached 67.9% (AUC 0.731). The paired bootstrap interval for the AUC gain of ridge with rolling features and Elo over Elo only is -0.002 to 0.015, which includes zero. For elastic net it is -0.001 to 0.012. Rolling features may add a small amount of discrimination, but this season cannot distinguish that from no gain. The two nonlinear models did not improve on the linear ones. Gradient boosting reached an AUC of 0.733 on the holdout, close to Elo only, and the untuned neural net reached 0.709, below Elo only (paired interval -0.039 to -0.006). With a few hundred mostly correlated features and noisy outcomes, there is little nonlinear structure for them to find, and the neural net likely overfits without tuning. Choosing the threshold on 2025 instead of using 0.5 changed holdout accuracy by at most 0.5 percentage points for any model. ![Holdout calibration by decile of predicted probability. The dashed line is perfect calibration.](../figures/holdout_calibration.png){#fig-calibration width=60%} Both models over-predict home wins in the lower deciles of predicted probability (@fig-calibration). This fits a lower home-win rate in 2025--26 (55.4%) than in the training seasons (58.5%). Each decile holds about 120 games, so single bins are noisy. ## Odds ratios To describe associations rather than predict, I fit the lean logistic model on 2002--2025, with and without Elo. Rate differences are scaled so that odds ratios are per percentage point. ::: {.cell tbl-cap='Odds ratios for a one-unit increase in each home-minus-away difference, fit on 2002--2025. Left: lean rolling model. Right: same model with Elo.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Term | OR [95% CI]| p| OR [95% CI]| p| |:------------------------------|-----------------------:|------:|-----------------------:|------:| |Net rating, 5 games | 1.0487 [1.0450, 1.0525]| <0.001| 1.0138 [1.0098, 1.0178]| <0.001| |Home ORtg - away DRtg, 5 games | 1.0078 [1.0038, 1.0119]| <0.001| 1.0078 [1.0037, 1.0120]| <0.001| |Off. rebound %, 5 games | 0.9934 [0.9887, 0.9982]| 0.007| 0.9994 [0.9945, 1.0043]| 0.806| |Turnover %, 5 games | 0.9874 [0.9772, 0.9977]| 0.016| 1.0052 [0.9945, 1.0160]| 0.344| |eFG%, 5 games | 1.0038 [0.9950, 1.0127]| 0.398| 0.9983 [0.9892, 1.0074]| 0.710| |Elo, season reset | --| --| 1.0022 [1.0017, 1.0028]| <0.001| |Elo, all time | --| --| 1.0029 [1.0026, 1.0033]| <0.001| ::: ::: Without Elo, a one-point advantage in five-game net rating is associated with 4.9% higher odds of a home win. Holding net rating fixed, higher offensive rebound and turnover percentages are associated with slightly *lower* odds. This is expected rather than meaningful: net rating already reflects rebounding and turnovers, so these terms describe how a given net rating was produced, not separate effects. The effective field-goal term is not distinguishable from zero. Once Elo is added, the rate terms are all indistinguishable from zero, net rating's odds ratio shrinks to 1.0138, and both Elo terms remain strongly associated with winning. # Changes from the course version The original paper (January 2026, kept in `reports/`) was written for a course. Rerunning its code on its own data snapshot reproduces its numbers. I found the following problems, which this version corrects. ::: {.cell tbl-cap='Course-version claims and what the code and corrected analysis show. Course numbers come from rerunning the original code on the January 2026 snapshot (2025 test season).'} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Issue Course version This version
Cross-validation Random 5-fold CV across 2002--2024; later seasons predicted earlier ones Rolling-origin validation by season
Tuned threshold Threshold tuned on the 2025 test season; reported 0.670 accuracy Threshold chosen on the 2025 validation season and applied to 2026; it changed accuracy by under one point
Data completeness Snapshot had 1,118 of 1,231 games in 2025 and 1,035 of 1,080 in 2021 Fresh pull with full seasons
Elo Described as not emphasized, but included in every penalized model and the inferential model Elo reported as its own baseline; it carries most of the signal
Inferential model Described as net rating, eFG%, and TOV%; text said shooting raised and turnovers lowered odds Five terms plus a version with Elo; eFG% and TOV% effects were not significant in the course model
Data source Cited as the NBA Stats API hoopR / SportsDataverse (ESPN box scores)
````` ::: ::: The course paper's headline numbers were not badly off: its 2025 holdout accuracy for ridge (0.662, AUC 0.714) is close to what the corrected method gives on complete 2025 data (0.665, AUC 0.721). The problems were in what the evaluation could support: the tuned-threshold result was not a test-set result, and the conclusion that rolling efficiency metrics drive predictions did not account for Elo. # Limitations - Only one holdout season. The 95% interval for single-season accuracy is about 5 percentage points wide. - Home-court advantage has drifted down over time. Models trained on all past seasons over-predict home wins in a season like 2025--26. - No rest, travel, injury, or roster information. Rolling team averages lag behind trades and injuries. - Elo settings ($K$, home advantage, reset rule) were not tuned. - Data comes from a third-party package. A few early seasons are missing games relative to the official schedule (for example, 1,224 of 1,229 in 2013), and missing games shift rolling windows. - Logistic and penalized linear models only. Tree ensembles were not compared. # Reproducibility The analysis is a `targets` pipeline [@landau2021targets] with packages pinned by `renv`. From a fresh clone with R 4.6: ``` renv::restore() targets::tar_make() ``` This rebuilds every table, figure, and this PDF from the saved data snapshot. Deleting the snapshot pulls fresh data through hoopR. The tests run with `Rscript tests/testthat.R`. # References {.unnumbered} ::: {#refs} :::
